The Story of the Thirty-Two Merchant Sons

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who illuminates the world and beyond, who sees and knows all things and teaches their true nature, and I write the story of the thirty-two merchant sons.

In Kaushambi, there were thirty-two merchants — Indradatt, Jindatt, Sagardatt, and others. Their sons were also thirty-two — Samudradatt, Vasumitra, Nagdatt, Jindas, and more. All of them were righteous, true devotees of Lord Jina, learned, virtuous, and adorned with the jewel of right faith. They had great friendship among themselves. This should be called the ripening of their merit — that all were wealthy, all were virtuous, all were righteous, and all had deep friendship with one another. Without merit, such a combination is never possible.

One day, all these friends went together to worship an omniscient yogi. They worshipped the Lord with devotion and then heard his sacred discourse on dharma. Upon asking the Lord, they learned that their lifespans were now very short. Realising that they should not let this final opportunity for the soul's welfare pass, they all took Jain initiation together.

Having taken initiation, they practised austerities and came to the banks of the Yamuna River. There they took the vow of sallekhana — the peaceful fast unto death. By fortune, heavy rains fell in those very days. Rivers and streams all overflowed. The Yamuna rose greatly. A powerful current came and swept all the monks away. In the end, they died in meditation and went to heaven. Truly, the character of great souls is far more steadfast than Mount Meru.

In heaven, enjoying divine pleasures, they remained ever absorbed in devotion to Lord Jinendra. May Lord Jinendra, the conqueror of karmas, always be victorious. May his pure teaching remain in the world forever and bring welfare to living beings. His supreme character, enduring many unbearable sufferings, stands firm like Mount Meru — none can compare with it. It is the highest ideal in the world, the destroyer of worldly wandering, the abode of supreme happiness, and the destroyer of the soul's enemies — delusion, anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, and aversion. It uproots them entirely.

O worthy souls! You too strive to attain this supreme ideal, so that you may become worthy of the supreme happiness of liberation. Lord Jinendra is capable of granting this to you.

This story teaches that the company of the righteous is a great blessing. The thirty-two friends, all virtuous and devoted, supported one another on the spiritual path. When they learned their time was short, they renounced the world together and attained liberation through united practice. The wise should seek the company of the righteous and walk the path of dharma together.
